Reader settings: (tap to change)

Type your Lexile any way it was given to you: 780, 780L, or BR100L. A range like 700–800L works too. Do not know it? Leave it blank. Save two or more books you read comfortably and the Stacks will estimate it. These settings stay on this device.

For grown-ups: how this works

Reading level. Each book shows a Lexile measure. Wilderland asks readers to choose books at their Lexile or higher, so with a level set, the Stacks treats 50L below to 100L above as "right at your level" and up to 250L above as "a real challenge." Books further above are left out of recommendations as too big a leap for now, and books below your level are left out while "Only books at my level or higher" is on. MetaMetrics, which makes the Lexile scale, describes a reader's comfortable range as about 100L below to 50L above their measure; Wilderland deliberately sets the bar higher. A ≈ before a Lexile means it has not yet been checked against a published list; confirm at hub.lexile.com. Graphic novels (GN) and poetry (NP) often have low or no Lexile measures however sophisticated they are.

Grades. The grade on each book is an editorial judgment about content (violence, language, mature themes), separate from reading difficulty. Each book carries a plain heads-up so families can decide. Books rated above the reader's grade are dimmed and kept out of recommendations unless the reader opts in.

Connections. Books are hand-tagged by genre, theme, kind of hero, plot shape and feeling, plus fan groupings for “readers also love.” Those groupings are editorial pairings, drawn from common read-alike lists, and are not sales or borrowing data.

Good company. Every claim about who read or picked a book is a real, documented fact, with the source named where one was checked for this site. Nothing is invented. Excerpts appear only for books in the public domain; other books link out to a preview. Cover images come from Open Library's cover service, matched by title and author and stored with this site; where none is found, or images are blocked, an emblem made for this site shows instead. Free-reading links appear only for books Open Library lists as public.

Nonfiction and Uncharted. Nonfiction books are grouped into 15 subject regions so students can explore informational reading as a world of its own. Each novel's page also suggests related true books. "Uncharted" marks books that break the usual rules in form or idea; it is an editorial judgment, and each one says why.

Life List and want-to-read. The Life List is Wilderland’s list of ways books can shape a life, to work through before graduation. Lines about awards, challenged books, publication dates and a few hand-checked facts (such as books adapted for TV) check themselves off when a matching book is on the reader’s shelf; award data was matched against Wikipedia’s winner lists in November 2026. Everything else is the reader’s own call, and any book can be added, including books not in the Stacks. Students who sign in with their school Google account have their shelf, want-to-read list and Life List saved to their account, so it follows them to any Chromebook.

Not for me. Readers can mark a book they read and didn't like, with optional reasons (too slow, too scary, too sad, too hard, too easy, not my kind of story, didn't like the ending). It stays on their shelf as read, counts toward the Life List, and pushes similar books down in every recommendation: shared fans, hero, plot and feel count against a book, and a reason aims at that one thing instead (too scary lowers spooky books, too hard lowers books at that level or above). Guides can see the list on the Student Roster.

The approach. The tone follows David Yeager's research on motivating ten-to-twenty-five-year-olds: young people respond to respect, real choice and honest stakes, and tune out lectures. So the site assigns nothing, awards no points, and tells readers the truth about what is in each book.
